definition.text: In economics, land means every naturally occurring resource, not just the ground itself.

facts.text: Examples include particular locations, mineral deposits, forests, fish stocks, air quality, geostationary orbits and parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Land is one of the three classic factors of production, alongside capital and labour.
Natural resources underlie the production of every good, including capital goods.
Income earned from owning or controlling natural resources is called rent.
Land's role was argued over at length in classical economics but became minor in 20th-century neoclassical economics.
In the UK, the non-produced asset of land makes up 51% of the country's total net worth.
Because nobody created land, it has no original owner, and rival claims to locations and mineral deposits have fed many civil wars and revolutions.

definition.text: Capital means durable goods that people have produced and then use to make further goods and services.

facts.text: A typical example is the machinery in a factory.
Unlike raw materials or energy, capital is not used up in one round of production but gives productive services over many cycles.
Economists treat capital as a factor of production alongside labour and land, a classification dating from classical economics.
Unlike land and non-renewable resources, capital can be produced or increased.
A nation's capital stock includes buildings, equipment, software and inventories, and modern usage also counts non-physical assets.
Capital goods are bought to make other goods, while consumer goods are bought to be consumed: a chocolate bar is a consumer good, the machine that makes it is capital.
Investment, or capital accumulation, means producing goods that are not consumed straight away but used to produce other goods.

definition.text: Economists divide capital into several kinds, including financial, social, instructional, human, public and natural capital.

facts.text: Financial capital is traded in financial markets, and its market value rests on expected revenues and risk rather than on money invested in the past.
Human capital broadly combines social, instructional and individual human talent.
Public capital covers government-owned infrastructure such as highways, water treatment, electric grids, hospitals and schools.
Natural capital is the world's stock of natural resources, and some of it gives people free goods and services called ecosystem services.

definition.text: Adam Smith split capital into fixed capital, which is not used up in making a product, and circulating capital, which is.

facts.text: Machines and storage buildings are fixed capital, while raw materials and intermediate products are circulating capital.
Smith also made clear that capital is a stock.
In Marx's theory, constant capital is spending on machinery and plant, while variable capital is spending on labour power, which he saw as the only source of surplus value.

definition.text: Factors of production are the inputs used to make goods and services, such as land, labour and capital.

facts.text: How much of each input is used determines output through a relationship called the production function.
One common list names four basic factors: land, labour, capital and the entrepreneur.
Land, labour and capital are primary factors; materials and energy are secondary because they come from the primary ones.
Primary factors help production without becoming part of the product or being much changed by it.
Adam Smith and David Ricardo saw the parts of a price as payments for land (rent), labour (wages) and capital.
The 18th-century French physiocrats held that a nation's wealth came only from land and agriculture.
Some economists, such as Robert Ayres and Benjamin Warr, fault orthodox economics for overlooking natural resources and declining resource capital.

title: Ecological factors of production

definition.text: Ecological economics replaces the usual factors of production with matter, energy and design intelligence, so that production obeys physical limits.

facts.text: Matter can be recycled but not created or destroyed, so there is an upper limit on how much material can be withdrawn and used.
Energy loses usefulness over time through entropy, as when electricity running a machine turns into heat.
At the maximum sustainable rates of matter and energy use, only better design can raise productivity.
This underlies a core claim of ecological economics: infinite growth is impossible.

distinct_from: Entrepreneurship as a factor of production

title: Entrepreneurship as a factor of production

definition.text: Entrepreneurship, the organising work of combining land, labour and capital to make a profit, is sometimes counted as a fourth factor of production.

facts.text: Some authors added it in the first half of the 20th century, and it became standard in the post-war neoclassical synthesis.
Many economists today instead treat human capital as the fourth factor, with entrepreneurship as a form of it.
Others have proposed energy, social capital or cultural heritage as additional factors.
